plan.title: Zero Velocity, Not Zero Acceleration: The Top of a Vertical Throw
plan.story:
Maya films her friend tossing a ball straight up and scrubs the video frame by frame. At one frame the ball hangs at the very top, perfectly still. "It isn't moving," she says, "so nothing is changing. The acceleration must be zero there." Her friend isn't convinced: "If nothing is changing, why does it fall in the next frame?" That disagreement is the question: at the highest point, is acceleration zero because velocity is zero?

First, the two words need to stay separate. Velocity is how fast the position changes, and in which direction. We call up positive, so a rising ball has positive velocity and a falling ball has negative velocity. Acceleration is how fast the velocity changes. It is not the velocity itself; it is the rate at which the velocity is being changed. A quantity can be zero at one instant while its rate of change is not. A swing at the end of its arc is momentarily at rest, yet it is already turning back.

Now work through a concrete throw. Ignore air resistance, so the only force on the ball after it leaves the hand is gravity, which pulls it down with acceleration g = 9.8 m/s^2. In the up-positive convention the acceleration is a = -9.8 m/s^2 the whole time. Launch the ball upward at 9.8 m/s from the release height, which we call height 0. Each second, gravity removes 9.8 m/s of upward velocity, so v = 9.8 - 9.8 t (in m/s, with t in seconds).

Step through the numbers:
At t = 0.0 s, v = +9.8 m/s (rising fast).
At t = 0.5 s, v = +4.9 m/s (rising, slower).
At t = 0.9 s, v = +0.98 m/s (barely rising).
At t = 1.0 s, v = 0 m/s (the top).
At t = 1.1 s, v = -0.98 m/s (barely falling).
At t = 1.5 s, v = -4.9 m/s (falling faster).
At t = 2.0 s, v = -9.8 m/s (back at release height, moving down as fast as it was thrown up).

Look at the change between neighbouring rows rather than the rows themselves. From 0.9 s to 1.0 s, velocity changes by -0.98 m/s. From 1.0 s to 1.1 s, it changes by -0.98 m/s again. Every 0.1 s interval in the whole flight, including the two that touch the top, shows the same change of -0.98 m/s. Dividing, -0.98 m/s per 0.1 s is -9.8 m/s^2. The acceleration at the top is exactly what it is everywhere else.

The peak height follows from the same numbers: the average velocity on the way up is (9.8 + 0) / 2 = 4.9 m/s, held for 1.0 s, so the ball rises 4.9 m above the release point.

On a velocity-time graph this becomes a picture. The velocity is a straight line sloping downward from +9.8 m/s to -9.8 m/s. It crosses the time axis at t = 1.0 s; that crossing is the top. The slope of the line is the acceleration, and a straight line has the same slope where it crosses zero as anywhere else. Being on the axis tells you the value is zero; it says nothing about the slope being zero.

Now test Maya's idea directly. Suppose the acceleration really did become zero at the top. Zero acceleration means the velocity stops changing. The velocity at that moment is zero, so it would stay zero, and the ball would hover in mid-air forever. The ball only falls because, at the top, its velocity is still being pushed toward negative values. The very fact that the next frame shows the ball lower is evidence of non-zero acceleration at the top.

So Maya's frame shows a ball with zero velocity, not zero acceleration. Gravity never switches off: it pulls down by the same 9.8 m/s^2 on the way up (slowing the ball), at the top (turning it around), and on the way down (speeding it up). The top is simply the instant when the steadily falling velocity passes through zero.
plan.cardDescription: Pause a thrown ball at its peak: velocity reads zero, yet the acceleration arrow and the v-t slope stay at 9.8 m/s² downward. No air resistance.
plan.learningGoal: Explain, using the constant slope of the velocity-time line and the equal velocity changes before and after the top, why the acceleration at the highest point is -9.8 m/s^2 and not zero even though the velocity there is zero.

scene.description: Left panel: vertical height axis y from 0 to 5.5 m (origin at release point, up positive) with a gridline and label at the 4.9 m peak. A ball moves on it; faint ghost dots mark its position every 0.1 s already elapsed. From the ball, a blue velocity arrow (scale 12 px per m/s, points up while rising, vanishes at the top, points down while falling) and a red acceleration arrow (separate scale 8 px per m/s^2, always 9.8 m/s^2 downward, same length every frame), drawn side by side. Each arrow carries its own scale label, so their lengths are not compared with each other. Right panel: velocity-time plot, t 0 to 2 s (origin at release), v from -10 to +10 m/s with a zero axis. The straight line v = 9.8 - 9.8t is traced up to the current time with a moving cursor dot. A slope triangle under the cursor spans the last 0.1 s and is labelled with its rise of -0.98 m/s. A dashed vertical guide marks t = 1.0 s (top). Readouts below: time, height, velocity, velocity change over last 0.1 s, acceleration. Both panels share the one timeline.

entities.label: Ball
entities.purpose: The thrown object, drawn at its current height on the height axis.

entities.label: Height axis
entities.purpose: Vertical scale from 0 to 5.5 m with the release point at 0 and the 4.9 m peak marked.

entities.label: Position trail
entities.purpose: Dots every 0.1 s showing spacing shrink near the top and grow on the way down.

entities.label: Velocity arrow
entities.purpose: Blue arrow on the ball, 12 px per m/s with its own scale label, showing the size and direction of velocity; zero length at the top.

entities.label: Acceleration arrow
entities.purpose: Red arrow on the ball, 8 px per m/s^2 with its own scale label, constant 9.8 m/s^2 downward at every instant including the top.

entities.label: Velocity-time plot
entities.purpose: Straight line of velocity against time whose constant slope is the acceleration.

entities.label: Slope triangle
entities.purpose: Shows the velocity change over the last 0.1 s at the cursor; it stays -0.98 m/s, including across the top.

entities.label: Top marker
entities.purpose: Dashed vertical line at t = 1.0 s where the plotted line crosses v = 0.

quantities.label: Time
quantities.meaning: Elapsed time since the ball left the hand.

quantities.label: Height
quantities.meaning: Height of the ball above the release point.
quantities.reference: y = 0 at release point, up positive.
quantities.relation: y equals 9.8 t minus 4.9 t squared; maximum 4.9 m at t = 1.0 s.

quantities.label: Velocity
quantities.relation: v equals 9.8 minus 9.8 t; zero at t = 1.0 s.

quantities.label: Acceleration
quantities.meaning: Rate of change of velocity, positive upward.
quantities.relation: Equals the slope of the velocity-time line.

quantities.label: Velocity change in last 0.1 s
quantities.meaning: Velocity now minus velocity 0.1 s earlier.
quantities.reference: Shown once t is at least 0.1 s.
quantities.relation: Always -0.98 m/s, which divided by 0.1 s gives -9.8 m/s^2.

observations.text: At t = 1.0 s the velocity readout is 0 m/s and the blue arrow vanishes, but the red arrow is unchanged and the acceleration readout still shows -9.8 m/s^2.
The velocity-time line is straight and crosses zero at the top marker without bending; the slope triangle shows -0.98 m/s per 0.1 s before, at and after the crossing.
Trail dots crowd together near 4.9 m and spread apart again as the ball descends, showing the velocity smoothly reversing rather than stopping.

checkpoints.label: Release
checkpoints.expected: Ball at height 0, long blue arrow up (9.8 m/s, 12 px per m/s), red arrow down (9.8 m/s^2, 8 px per m/s^2), each with its own scale label; plot cursor at +9.8 m/s.

checkpoints.label: Just before top
checkpoints.expected: Height 4.85 m, velocity +0.98 m/s with a short blue up arrow, velocity change -0.98 m/s, acceleration -9.8 m/s^2, red arrow unchanged.

checkpoints.label: Top
checkpoints.expected: Height 4.9 m, velocity 0 m/s and no blue arrow, red arrow still 9.8 m/s^2 down, cursor on the v = 0 axis at the dashed top marker, slope triangle still -0.98 m/s.

checkpoints.label: Just after top
checkpoints.expected: Height 4.85 m, velocity -0.98 m/s with a short blue down arrow, velocity change -0.98 m/s, acceleration -9.8 m/s^2.

checkpoints.label: Back at release height
checkpoints.expected: Ball at height 0, blue arrow down at 9.8 m/s, red arrow unchanged; full straight line from +9.8 to -9.8 m/s on the plot.

mode.initialState: Paused at t = 0 s: ball at the release point (height 0), blue velocity arrow pointing up at 9.8 m/s, red acceleration arrow pointing down at 9.8 m/s^2, empty trail, plot cursor at +9.8 m/s with no line yet drawn, velocity-change readout showing a dash until 0.1 s has elapsed.

controls.label: Playback
controls.purpose: Run the throw from release to return so the learner sees the velocity arrow shrink, vanish and reverse while the acceleration arrow never changes.
controls.selectionReason: The answer depends on how velocity changes through time, so a timeline is essential; Play, Pause and Replay are the native transport for it.

controls.label: Time since release
controls.purpose: Seek to exactly 0.9 s, 1.0 s and 1.1 s to compare velocity and acceleration just before, at and after the top.
controls.selectionReason: Freezing the precise instant of the top, as Maya did with her video, is the heart of the question; playback alone passes it too quickly.

assumptions: No air resistance: after release the only force is gravity, giving a constant acceleration of 9.8 m/s^2 downward.
Motion is purely vertical with up taken as positive, so acceleration is -9.8 m/s^2 throughout.
The ball is launched at 9.8 m/s upward from height 0 and the scene ends when it returns to height 0 at t = 2.0 s; the catch or landing is not modelled.
limitations: Launch speed is fixed, so the learner cannot vary it; the conclusion that acceleration is unchanged at the top holds for any launch speed, which the story states but the scene does not test.
Real throws have air drag, which slightly changes the acceleration magnitude on the way up and down; the scene ignores it.
The hand's push before release is not shown; the scene begins after the ball has left the hand.

claims.text: With launch speed 9.8 m/s and g = 9.8 m/s^2, velocity is v = 9.8 - 9.8 t and is zero at t = 1.0 s.
The peak height is 4.9 m above the release point.
Every 0.1 s interval, including 0.9 to 1.0 s and 1.0 to 1.1 s, has a velocity change of -0.98 m/s, giving -9.8 m/s^2.
If acceleration were zero at the instant velocity is zero, the velocity would remain zero and the ball would not fall.
claims.check: Zero rate of change applied to v = 0 leaves v = 0 for all later times, contradicting the observed fall.

carried: At cpStart, check that the blue (117.6 px) and red (78.4 px) arrows sit side by side, that each shows its own scale label, and that they don't overlap the trail or the height labels.
At cpTop, check that the blue arrow is gone, that the red arrow keeps its length, that the cursor sits on v = 0 at the dashed guide, and that the readouts show 0.00 m/s and -9.8 m/s^2.
